lesson.title: Before Birth: What Embryos Reveal, and What They Do Not
lesson.summary: Comparing the early developmental stages of different vertebrate species reveals shared structures not visible in the adult body, evidence of a deeply conserved developmental toolkit inherited from a common ancestor, though not, as an old and discredited idea once claimed, a literal replay of evolutionary history.
lesson.body:
Comparative anatomy, covered a few chapters back, mostly compares adult structures. Comparative embryology extends the same basic idea, looking for shared structure that points to common ancestry, backward into development, comparing the embryos of different species at similar early stages, before the differences that separate the adult forms have fully appeared.

The clearest example involves a set of structures called pharyngeal, or branchial, pouches and arches, folds and grooves that appear in the neck and throat region of essentially every vertebrate embryo early in development, including fish, chickens, pigs, and humans. In fish, these embryonic structures develop into gills. In humans and other mammals, who never develop gills or breathe underwater, the very same embryonic starting structures develop into something quite different: parts of the jaw, several small bones of the middle ear, and portions of the throat and neck. Vertebrate embryos, including human embryos, also pass through an early stage with a visible tail extending past where the legs will form, later reduced, in humans, into that same coccyx discussed as a vestigial structure in the last chapter. The organisms that develop from these embryos end up looking nothing alike, but the underlying embryonic starting material, and much of the genetic machinery directing how it folds and grows, is shared.

It is worth being precise here, because this is a topic where a well known but incorrect idea from the history of evolutionary thought still circulates. In the 1800s, the German biologist Ernst Haeckel proposed that embryonic development literally replays an organism's evolutionary history in compressed form, an idea summarized as ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny, and illustrated it with embryo drawings that exaggerated the similarities between species. That strong claim, that a human embryo passes through a fish stage, then a reptile stage, and so on, is not correct, and Haeckel's drawings substantially overstated how similar different species' embryos actually are at comparable stages. Modern comparative embryology makes a more modest and better supported claim: early embryos of related species share structures and developmental pathways because those pathways were inherited, with modification, from a common ancestor, not because development is a literal rerun of adult ancestral forms. The shared pharyngeal arches are a real, well documented homology. A human embryo growing gill slits and briefly becoming a fish is not.

With that correction in place, the evidence comparative embryology does provide is genuinely strong, and it strengthens the case built in earlier chapters rather than replacing it. The same deeply conserved genes that pattern the body plan during early development, including a family of genes called Hox genes that help establish which body regions become head, thorax, limbs, and so on, are shared with only modest changes across enormously different animal groups. That a shared genetic and developmental toolkit, not just shared adult anatomy, underlies such different final body forms is difficult to explain except as inheritance from a distant common ancestor, further echoing the anatomical evidence from earlier in this unit and anticipating the molecular evidence covered next.
